text: Service configuration management practice. This practice is the idea behind every CMDB you'll ever touch -- but it starts as a concept, not a tool.

ITIL 4's purpose statement for this practice is precise: ensure accurate, reliable information about the configuration of services, and the configuration items that support them, is available when and where it's needed. That's not 'maintain a database.' It's 'make sure the right people can trust the right information, at the moment they need it.' The database is just the tool that makes that possible at real scale -- a team of three can hold this in their heads, but an organization running hundreds of services cannot.

A configuration item, or CI, is anything that needs to be managed to deliver a service. That's intentionally broad. A server is a CI. The application on it is a CI. A network switch is a CI. Some organizations track documentation -- a disaster recovery runbook, a contract -- as a CI, and some even track a role, like 'on-call database administrator,' because a service depends on that role being filled. The real test isn't what category of thing it is. It's whether losing track of it puts the service at risk.

A list of CIs by itself is just an inventory. What makes this practice powerful is capturing the relationships between CIs -- this application runs on this server, which depends on this network device. That relationship graph is what turns a flat list into something you can actually reason with: impact analysis when something fails, and root-cause investigation when an incident keeps recurring across what looked like unrelated services.

Think back to Chapter 4. Incident management needed to know what else a failing component might affect. Problem management needed to trace a recurring incident back to a shared root cause. Change enablement needed to assess the blast radius of a proposed change before approving it. All three consume configuration data and the relationship graph behind it -- none of them generate it themselves. Remove this practice, and all three quietly degrade.

Configuration management tracks a CI for its role in delivering a service. Next, we'll look at the same physical item -- tracked for an entirely different reason: its financial and contractual value, through IT asset management.
